entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16807"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen33112" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1-1Cor.4.21">1Co 4:1-21</reference>. True View of Ministers: The Judgment Is Not to Be Forestalled; Meanwhile the Apostles' Low State Contrasts with the Corinthians' Party Pride, Not That Paul Would Shame Them, but as a Father Warn Them; for Which End He Sent Timothy, and Will Soon Come Himself.<div eID="gen33112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16807"/><hi type="bold">1. account ... us--</hi>Paul and Apollos.<div eID="gen33113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ministers of Christ--</hi>not heads of the Church in whom ye are severally to glory (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>); the headship belongs to Christ alone; we are but His servants ministering to you (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">1Co 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen33114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stewards--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.12.42">Lu 12:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1Pe 4:10</reference>). Not the depositories of grace, but dispensers of it ("rightly dividing" or dispensing it), so far as God gives us it, to others. The chazan, or "overseer," in the synagogue answered to the bishop or "angel" of the Church, who called seven of the synagogue to read the law every sabbath, and oversaw them. The parnasin of the synagogue, like the ancient "deacon" of the Church, took care of the poor (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.1-Acts.6.7">Ac 6:1-7</reference>) and subsequently preached in subordination to the presbyters or bishops, as Stephen and Philip did. The Church is not the appendage to the priesthood; but the minister is the steward of God to the Church. Man shrinks from too close contact with God; hence he willingly puts a priesthood between, and would serve God by deputy. The pagan (like the modern Romish) priest was rather to conceal than to explain "the mysteries of God." The minister's office is to "preach" (literally, "proclaim as a herald," <reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">Mt 10:27</reference>) the deep truths of God ("mysteries," heavenly truths, only known by revelation), so far as they have been revealed, and so far as his hearers are disposed to receive them. Josephus says that the Jewish religion made known to all the people the mysteries of their religion, while the pagans concealed from all but the "initiated" few, the mysteries of theirs. <div eID="gen33115" type="x-p"/>

The parnasin of the synagogue, like the ancient "deacon" of the Church, took care of the poor ( Ac 6:1-7 ) and subsequently preached in subordination to the presbyters or bishops, as Stephen and Philip did. The Church is not the appendage to the priesthood; but the minister is the steward of God to the Church. Man shrinks from too close contact with God; hence he willingly puts a priesthood between, and would serve God by deputy. The pagan (like the modern Romish) priest was rather to conceal than to explain "the mysteries of God." The minister's office is to "preach" (literally, "proclaim as a herald," Mt 10:27 ) the deep truths of God ("mysteries," heavenly truths, only known by revelation), so far as they have been revealed, and so far as his hearers are disposed to receive them. Josephus says that the Jewish religion made known to all the people the mysteries of their religion, while the pagans concealed from all but the "initiated" few, the mysteries of theirs.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16808"/><div sID="gen33116" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16808"/><hi type="bold">2. Moreover--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Moreover here" (that is, on earth). The contrast thus is between man's usage as to stewards (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">1Co 4:2</reference>), and God's way (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3">1Co 4:3</reference>). Though here below, in the case of stewards, inquiry is made, that one man be found (that is, proved to be) faithful; yet God's steward awaits no such judgment of man, in man's day, but the Lord's judgment in His great day. Another argument against the Corinthians for their partial preferences of certain teachers for their gifts: whereas what God requires in His stewards is faithfulness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.20">1Sa 3:20</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.5">He 3:5</reference>); as indeed is required in earthly stewards, but with this difference (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3">1Co 4:3</reference>), that God's stewards await not man's judgment to test them, but the testing which shall be in the day of the Lord. <div eID="gen33116" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16809"/><div sID="gen33117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16809"/><hi type="bold">3. it is a very small thing--</hi>literally, "it amounts to a very small matter"; not that I despise your judgment, but as compared with God's, it almost comes to nothing.<div eID="gen33117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judged ... of man's judgment--</hi>literally, "man's day," contrasted with the day (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13">1Co 3:13</reference>) of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.4">1Th 5:4</reference>). "The day of man" is here put before us as a person [Wahl]. All days previous to the day of the Lord are man's days. Emesti translates the thrice recurring Greek for "judged ... judge ... judgeth" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.4">1Co 4:4</reference>), thus: To me for my part (though capable of being found faithful) it is a very small matter that I should be approved of by man's judgment; yea, I do not even assume the right of judgment and approving myself--but He that has the right, and is able to judge on my case (the Dijudicator), is the Lord. <div eID="gen33118" type="x-p"/>

Here all judgments in general are forbidden, which would, on our part, presumptuously forestall God's prerogative of final judgment.<div eID="gen33123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>Jesus Christ, whose "ministers" we are (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">1Co 4:1</reference>), and who is to be the judge (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.42">Ac 10:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">17:31</reference>).<div eID="gen33124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manifest ... hearts--</hi>Our judgments now (as those of the Corinthians respecting their teachers) are necessarily defective; as we only see the outward act, we cannot see the motives of "hearts." "Faithfulness" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">1Co 4:2</reference>) will hereby be estimated, and the "Lord" will "justify," or the reverse (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.4">1Co 4:4</reference>), according to the state of the heart.<div eID="gen33125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then shall every man have praise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.8">1Co 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.23">1Sa 26:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.21">Mt 25:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.28">23, 28</reference>). Rather, "his due praise," not exaggerated praise, such as the Corinthians heaped on favorite teachers; "the praise" (so the Greek) due for acts estimated by the motives. "Then," not before: therefore wait till then (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.7">Jas 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33126" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16814"/><div sID="gen33133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16814"/>8. Irony. Translate, "Already ye are filled full (with spiritual food), already ye are rich, ye have seated yourselves upon your throne as kings, without us." The emphasis is on "already" and "without us"; ye act as if ye needed no more to "hunger and thirst after righteousness," and as if already ye had reached the "kingdom" for which Christians have to strive and suffer. Ye are so puffed up with your favorite teachers, and your own fancied spiritual attainments in knowledge through them, that ye feel like those "filled full" at a feast, or as a "rich" man priding himself in his riches: so ye feel ye can now do "without us," your first spiritual fathers (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">1Co 4:15</reference>). They forgot that before the "kingdom" and the "fulness of joy," at the marriage feast of the Lamb, must come the cross, and suffering, to every true believer (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.5">2Ti 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.12">11, 12</reference>). They were like the self-complacent Laodiceans (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Re 3:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Ho 12:8</reference>). Temporal fulness and riches doubtless tended in some cases at Corinth, to generate this spiritual self-sufficiency; the contrast to the apostle's literal "hunger and thirst" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">1Co 4:11</reference>) proves this.<div eID="gen33133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I would ... ye did reign--</hi>Translate, "I would indeed," &c. I would truly it were so, and that your kingdom had really begun.<div eID="gen33134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we also might reign with you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2Co 12:14</reference>). "I seek not yours, but you." Your spiritual prosperity would redound to that of us, your fathers in Christ (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.23">1Co 9:23</reference>). When you reach the kingdom, you shall be our "crown of rejoicing, in the presence of our Lord Jesus" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen33135" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 8. Irony. Translate, "Already ye are filled full (with spiritual food), already ye are rich, ye have seated yourselves upon your throne as kings, without us." The emphasis is on "already" and "without us"; ye act as if ye needed no more to "hunger and thirst after righteousness," and as if already ye had reached the "kingdom" for which Christians have to strive and suffer. Ye are so puffed up with your favorite teachers, and your own fancied spiritual attainments in knowledge through them, that ye feel like those "filled full" at a feast, or as a "rich" man priding himself in his riches: so ye feel ye can now do "without us," your first spiritual fathers ( 1Co 4:15 ). They forgot that before the "kingdom" and the "fulness of joy," at the marriage feast of the Lamb, must come the cross, and suffering, to every true believer ( 2Ti 2:5 , 11, 12 ). They were like the self-complacent Laodiceans ( Re 3:17 ; compare Ho 12:8 ). Temporal fulness and riches doubtless tended in some cases at Corinth, to generate this spiritual self-sufficiency; the contrast to the apostle's literal "hunger and thirst" ( 1Co 4:11 ) proves this. I would ... ye did reign-- Translate, "I would indeed," &c. I would truly it were so, and that your kingdom had really begun. that we also might reign with you-- ( 2Co 12:14 ). "I seek not yours, but you." Your spiritual prosperity would redound to that of us, your fathers in Christ ( 1Co 9:23 ). When you reach the kingdom, you shall be our "crown of rejoicing, in the presence of our Lord Jesus" ( 1Th 2:19 ).

For--</hi>assigning the reason for desiring that the "reign" of himself and his fellow apostles with the Corinthians were come; namely, the present afflictions of the former.<div eID="gen33136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I think--</hi>The Corinthians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">1Co 3:18</reference>) "seemed" to (literally, as here, "thought") themselves "wise in this world." Paul, in contrast, "thinks" that God has sent forth him and his fellow ministers "last," that is, the lowest in this world. The apostles fared worse than even the prophets, who, though sometimes afflicted, were often honored (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.10">2Ki 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.9">5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen33137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set forth--</hi>as a spectacle or gazing-stock.<div eID="gen33138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">us the apostles--</hi>Paul includes Apollos with the apostles, in the broader sense of the word; so <reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">2Co 8:23</reference> (Greek for "messengers," apostles).<div eID="gen33139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it were appointed to death--</hi>as criminals condemned to die.<div eID="gen33140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made a spectacle--</hi>literally, "a theatrical spectacle." So the Greek in <reference osisRef="Heb.10.33">He 10:33</reference>, "made a gazing-stock by reproaches and afflictions." Criminals "condemned to die," in Paul's time, were exhibited as a gazing-stock to amuse the populace in the amphitheater. They were "set forth last" in the show, to fight with wild beasts. This explains the imagery of Paul here. (Compare Tertullian [On Modesty, 14]).<div eID="gen33141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the world--</hi>to the whole world, including "both angels and men"; "the whole family in heaven and earth" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">Ep 3:15</reference>). As Jesus was "seen of angels" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), so His followers are a spectacle to the holy angels who take a deep interest in all the progressive steps of redemption (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>). Paul tacitly implies that though "last" and lowest in the world's judgment, Christ's servants are deemed by angels a spectacle worthy of their most intense regard [Chrysostom]. However, since "the world" is a comprehensive expression, and is applied in this Epistle to the evil especially (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>), and since the spectators (in the image drawn from the amphitheater) gaze at the show with savage delight, rather than with sympathy for the sufferers, I think bad angels are included, besides good angels. Estius makes the bad alone to be meant. But the generality of the term "angels," and its frequent use in a good sense, as well as <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>, incline me to include good as well as bad angels, though, for the reasons stated above, the bad may be principally meant. <div eID="gen33142" type="x-p"/>

How much your lot (supposing it real) is to be envied, and ours to be pitied.<div eID="gen33143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fools--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1Co 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">3:18</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.18">Ac 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.24">26:24</reference>).<div eID="gen33144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for Christ's sake ... in Christ--</hi>Our connection with Christ only entails on us the lowest ignominy, "ON ACCOUNT OF," or, "FOR THE SAKE OF" Him, as "fools"; yours gives you full fellowship IN Him as "wise" (that is, supposing you really are all you seem, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">1Co 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen33145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we ... weak ... ye ... strong--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.3">1Co 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.9">2Co 13:9</reference>).<div eID="gen33146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we ... despised--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>) because of our "weakness," and our not using worldly philosophy and rhetoric, on account of which ye Corinthians and your teachers are (seemingly) so "honorable." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16818"/><div sID="gen33151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16818"/><hi type="bold">12. working with our own hands--</hi>namely, "even unto this present hour" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">1Co 4:11</reference>). This is not stated in the narrative of Paul's proceedings at Ephesus, from which city he wrote this Epistle (though it is expressly stated of him at Corinth, compare <reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19">19</reference>). But in his address to the Ephesian elders at Miletus (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.34">Ac 20:34</reference>), he says, "Ye yourselves know that these hands have ministered unto my necessities," &c. The undesignedness of the coincidence thus indirectly brought out is incompatible with forgery. <div eID="gen33151" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16823"/><div sID="gen33160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16823"/><hi type="bold">17. For this came--</hi>that ye may the better "be followers of me" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.16">1Co 4:16</reference>), through his admonitions.<div eID="gen33160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent ... Timotheus--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1Co 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.21">Ac 19:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">22</reference>). "Paul purposed ... when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem. So he sent into Macedonia Timotheus and Erastus." Here it is not expressly said that he sent Timothy into Achaia (of which Corinth was the capital), but it is implied, for he sent him with Erastus before him. As he therefore purposed to go into Achaia himself, there is every probability they were to go thither also. They are said only to have been sent into Macedonia, because it was the country to which they went immediately from Ephesus. The undesignedness of the coincidence establishes the genuineness of both the Epistle and the history. In both, Timothy's journey is closely connected with Paul's own (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.19">1Co 4:19</reference>). Erastus is not specified in the Epistle, probably because it was Timothy who was charged with Paul's orders, and possibly Erastus was a Corinthian, who, in accompanying Timothy, was only returning home. The seeming discrepancy at least shows that the passages were not taken from one another [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ].<div eID="gen33161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son--</hi>that is, converted by me (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">1Co 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.6">Ac 14:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.7">7</reference>; with <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.2">2Ti 1:2</reference>).
